en: This *Jiǎngjǔ Zuǎnshì* (Compendium of Explanations on the *Jiǎngjǔ*) relies solely on ancient commentaries and the original treatise; consequently, students find it difficult to enter its depths.

At present, there exist works such as the *Zhèngyì* (Verification of Meaning) and the *Jíjiě* (Collected Explanations), yet these also contain mutual discrepancies. Thus, students still find it difficult to determine which to adopt.

This current compendium takes the ancient supplementary notes as its primary basis, while cross-referencing the two aforementioned schools and the explanatory texts of the original treatise to synthesize them into a coherent, unified system.
I have consulted the *Zhijie* (Direct Explanation), wherein the detailed and the concise mutually support one another to illuminate each other.

However, as this work focuses exclusively on the objects of cognition (*ālambana-pramāṇa*), and since the mental factors (*caitta*) and their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are already fully contained within the *Bai fa zuan* (Compendium of the Hundred Dharmas), they are not repeated here. This serves to avoid excessive verbosity and tediousness.
Nevertheless, every word has its source and is entirely not my own invention; it would be a false act to plagiarize them as my own view. This was written by Guangyi, a novice attendant.

Regarding the Dharma-gate of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), this elder has instructed me on the point of entry for investigation, so that by examining it once, one may see its stability and correctness.
If every word is taken to heart, then one's understanding will not err; therefore, I have carefully collated these references to prevent forgetfulness.
This is not intended as a presentation to the great masters.
Hand-corrected by the seventy-seven-year-old elder Hanshan on a summer day in the *Renxu* year of the Tianqi era.
Compiled and annotated by Guangyi at Wuru Peak on Mount Kuang, Ming Dynasty. *Annotated Explanation of the Verses on the Eight Consciousnesses*.

The eight consciousnesses are: first, the eye-consciousness; second, the ear-consciousness; third, the nose-consciousness; fourth, the tongue-consciousness; fifth, the body-consciousness; sixth, the mental-consciousness;
seventh, the *manas*-consciousness; and eighth, the *ālaya*-consciousness. The first six derive their names from their bases (*āśraya*);

the seventh establishes its designation through its associated mental factors (*samprayukta*); and the eighth receives its title according to its functional capacity (*vṛtti*). This is explained in the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*. Regarding the "rules" (*niyama*), first—

When Master Xuanzang completed his compilation of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Dharma Master Kuiji—being a disciple of Master Xuanzang—observed that the ten-fascicle original treatise was voluminous in text and profound in meaning.
He therefore requested that Master Xuanzang compile its essential doctrines, naming it the *Ji shi song* (Verses on the Collection of [Essential] Teachings).
This work collects the meanings of all dharmas to bestow them upon sentient beings; it divides the eight consciousnesses into four chapters.

Each chapter contains twelve verses. By assigning each of the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*) to their respective positions within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), they are categorized according to their varying degrees of presence or absence without any confusion; thus, they are called "rules" (*niyama*).
Although the treatise consists of ten fascicles, its entire meaning is fully encompassed by these forty-eight verses without omission. It may truly be called the most concise and essential.

It serves as the key to the entire Great Canon of the Buddha’s teachings. Not only do lecturers fail to understand it and thus find it difficult to penetrate the framework of the doctrine, but even practitioners of Zen who do not comprehend this will remain ignorant of the number of times their own minds arise and cease.
It is what is called the very essence of the Buddha-dharma. This is because the perfectly luminous and wondrous mind of the single true Dharma-realm is fundamentally devoid of even a single thing.

All phenomena are fundamentally devoid of the characteristics of body, mind, or the world; how, then, could there be the shadow-like conditions of deluded discrimination arising from the opposition between sense organs and their objects?
Fundamentally, this mind and its objects both arise from the non-awakening of ignorance, which causes one to be deluded regarding this single True Dharma-realm.
The unarisen and undying true mind, through its conjunction with the arising-and-ceasing [phenomena], transforms into the *ālaya-vijñāna*.

Based on this consciousness, the two divisions of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) arise. Therefore, the seeing-part is the mind and the image-part is the object.

Thus, those who discriminate between beauty and ugliness or engage in acceptance and rejection based on objects are merely deluded consciousnesses. If one realizes that mind and objects are nothing but consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), then discrimination will not arise;
the single mind will be perfectly luminous, forever free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). At present, because one has not yet awakened to the single mind, [this is so].

One must first understand that the mind and its objects are merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*). Then, the arising and ceasing of mental activities will immediately vanish, and one can enter into the single mind.
This verse outlines the general framework by singling out the time when the eight consciousnesses, as the sovereign mind-kings, perceive objects.

Because objects have qualities of beauty or ugliness, the mental factors (*caitta*) associated with them grasp these qualities, giving rise to hatred and love, or acceptance and rejection. Consequently, one performs good or evil deeds. [The text continues: Good...

Because evil serves as the cause, it brings about the two retributions of suffering and pleasure as its fruit. However, these eight consciousnesses, the sovereign minds (*cittarāja*), are fundamentally neither good nor evil.
It is rather the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*) that assist the sovereign mind in performing actions to create good and evil karma.
Thus, through the power of karma, sentient beings are drawn toward and experience suffering and pleasure; this is the law of birth and death for living beings.
This is all there is. Within this, the eight consciousnesses are enumerated, each possessing a different number of mental factors (*caitta*) and differing in the strength of their karmic formation.
These distinctions are clearly set forth so that students may investigate and fully understand the point of arising and ceasing, making it easy to regulate and transform them.
This is because the seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing of sentient beings in their daily lives—

The mind that is free from objects. This cognizing mind possesses three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
Regarding "direct perception": "direct" (*prati*) means manifesting; "perception" (*akṣa*) means measuring.

Because it is vividly present in the first moment, it does not give rise to conceptual construction, is devoid of verbal designations, lacks a deliberative mind, and directly apprehends the essence of the phenomenon, like a mirror.
Manifest perception (*pratyakṣa*). For example, upon seeing a mountain one knows it is a mountain; upon seeing water one knows it is water.

This occurs without relying on conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), and is therefore called manifest perception. As for inference (*anumāna*), it is knowing something to be so by means of comparison and measurement.
For instance, seeing a horn over a wall, one knows there is an ox there; seeing smoke across a mountain, one knows there is fire there. This is based on the principle of concomitance.
When the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) follows what is seen and immediately engages in conceptualization, it belongs to inference (anumāna).

It is called "inference" because there is a process of comparative measurement. As for that which is "not a valid cognition" (apramāṇa): when the mind takes an object as its condition, if it involves erroneous and false conceptualization regarding that object such that it cannot know it correctly, and the object does not correspond to the mind, it is termed "not a valid cognition. These three types of valid cognition are those that possess the capacity to cognize their objects.

It is the mind (*citta*). Furthermore, the objects (*ālambana*) it perceives are also of three kinds: namely, the objective realm (*tattva-viṣaya*), the realm with a shared substance (*sābhāsa-viṣaya*), and the realm of solitary images (*pratibimba-mātra-viṣaya*).
As for the objective realm, it is that which is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The term "objective" (*tattva*) signifies reality.

This means that the fundamental dharmas of the sense faculties and their objects are, in their essence, the wondrous nature of *tathatā* (suchness). They are neither beautiful nor ugly, because the perceiving mind is free from conceptual discrimination. Thus, the object—
The absence of beauty or ugliness constitutes the objective realm (*svabhāva-viṣaya*). The verse states: "The objective realm does not follow the mind.

This means that these *nimitta-bhāga*s (objective aspects), such as the sense faculties and their objects, are all produced from actual seeds; they do not arise from the seeds of the *darśana-bhāga* (subjective perceiving aspect) that takes them as its object.

Therefore, this objective realm has the five real sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) as its substance, for it is constituted by the eight factors consisting of both the subject and the object. As for the "aspect with substance" (*sadravya-nimitta*), it is [analogical]...

Regarding the objects of cognition (*ālambana-pramāṇa*): those objects that carry a substantial nature (*sadravya*) may be either real or similar [to the real], because the sixth and seventh consciousnesses each have their own respective objects.
When the six consciousnesses externally perceive the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), they infer characteristics such as long and short, square and round, beautiful and ugly, and so forth.
It belongs to the conceptualization of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the second moment; therefore, it is an inference (*anumāna*).

Because these characteristics such as length and so forth arise as transformations that carry the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of that external object, they are called "apparently carrying the essence" (*sādṛśyopādāna*).

Since this is provisional (*prajñapti*), it is said that when the mind takes form (*rūpa*) as its object, it is "apparently carrying the essence. The intermediate *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) arises from one end; that is to say, it arises solely from the subjective capacity (*grāhaka*).

Because it arises conditioned by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), there are two types of "solitary shadows" (*kevala-chāyā*): those with a real object (*sadravya*) and those without a real object (*adravya*).

When the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes as its object the past, fallen-away shadows of the five sensory objects, it is called a "solitary shadow with a real object," and it is also termed "resembling a shadow with a real substrate" (*sadṛśa-sad-vastuka*).

If the mental consciousness takes as its object things such as flowers in the sky or the horns of a rabbit, it is called a "solitary shadow without a real object. This includes both [types of] "resembling a shadow with a real substrate."

Those without substance and those that are mere shadows are all transformations of the imagined object-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) produced by the seeing-aspect (darśana-bhāga) of the perceiving consciousness;

therefore, it is said that "mere shadows arise solely from the seeing-aspect. These three [types of objects] take as their essence the imagined object-aspect transformed by the seeing-aspect of the sixth consciousness.

Regarding the "truly possessing the objective essence" (zhēndài zhì jìng): this refers precisely to the mind taking the mind as its object. Therefore it is said: "The mind taking the mind as its object is truly possessing the objective essence;

the intermediate *nimitta-bhāga* arises from both ends. This means that when the seven consciousnesses take the *darśana-bhāga* of the eighth consciousness as the self (*ātman*), that *nimitta-bhāga* does not arise from a separate seed.
One half arises from the same seed as the original essence (*bhūtārtha*) which is the object of the eighth consciousness. The other...
Half [of these] arise from the same seed as the seventh consciousness’s *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect).

Those arising from the *svabhāva* (essential nature) are of an unobscured nature (*anivṛta*), while those arising from the *darśana-bhāga* are of an obscured nature (*nivṛta*). Because both categories are subsumed within the indeterminate, it is said:

"The 'substantially associated' (*saviṣaya*) is pervasive of the mental states (*caitta*). This is called "true association" because the object and the subject are transformed by the same single *darśana-bhāga*.
This is the distinction between the substance [of the mind] and its objects. When the mind and its objects are treated as opposites, the objects may be adverse or favorable, beautiful or ugly;

consequently, the perceiving mind arises in response to them, giving rise to hatred and love, acceptance and rejection, and so forth. Thus, one gives rise to delusions and creates karma, becoming defiled by the two natures of good and evil.
This results in the experience of the two retributions of suffering and pleasure in the future. Therefore, the sovereign mind possesses...
Regarding painful sensations and pleasant sensations: if neither wholesome nor unwholesome states arise, they belong to the indeterminate nature and are thus neutral sensations (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

For this reason, sensation is also threefold. Consequently, that sentient beings within the three realms—whether ascending or descending, rising or sinking, revolving through saṃsāra, and never forgetting suffering or pleasure—all do so because mental objects and the mind are initiated by the internal habit-energies (*vāsanā*) transforming within consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). It is due to these three measures and three... [text fragment].

Because of objects, the three natures, and the three types of sensation, one cannot transcend birth and death; all of this is the fault of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Thus, the treatise says: "Sentient beings revolve depending upon mind, thought, and consciousness. Now, according to the Yogācāra school, ordinary people in their daily lives do not realize who creates or who experiences suffering and pleasure.
Non-Buddhists falsely posit a divine self (*ātman*), while those of the Two Vehicles [view things] as being outside the mind.
Therefore, the Buddha taught that "all phenomena are but consciousness" (*vijñapti-mātra*) so that one may know that nothing exists apart from one's own mind.

Since the mind does not perceive the mind, there are no characteristics (*nimitta*) to be grasped; this is precisely to lead the student directly to the realization that their own mind is fundamentally devoid of such things.
Now, as for the fact that the verses on the eight consciousnesses are called "rules" (*vidhi*), they merely serve to elucidate the nature of the mind and its objects. Its...

All that is performed, whether wholesome or unwholesome, is accomplished through the assistance of mental factors (*caitta*). Because these factors vary in their respective abundance or scarcity, their power is correspondingly strong or weak;
this is the general outline of the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*). The mental factors have already been examined in the "One Hundred Dharmas" (*śata-dharma*).

Here, I shall list them in advance along with their objects (*ālambana*), so that when we encounter them in the text, there will be no need for further detailed explanation, lest it hinder the contemplation of the mind.
○ The Verse on the Five Consciousnesses:
"The nature of the object is real; it is direct perception (pratyakṣa) and permeates the three moral natures.
These twelve lines below constitute the verse on the five evolving consciousnesses—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. The first line begins [the exposition].

Verses on the Scope of the Objects of the Five Consciousnesses and the Three Natures. Question: Regarding the five preceding evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) in their state prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), to which of the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do they definitively belong?

And to which of the three types of objects (*viṣaya*) do they definitively belong? Answer: The type of valid cognition of the first five consciousnesses belongs to direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*).

Their objects belong to the category of objective reality (*paratantra-svabhāva*). This is because the five consciousnesses are of the same substance as the eighth [consciousness]. When they take an object, [they perceive it directly].

This belongs exclusively to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The first five evolving consciousnesses are the manifestation of the lucid essence of the eight consciousnesses at the gates of the five sense organs;
they function to cognize objects. At the very moment the object is first reflected, this constitutes the first moment of thought, before any discrimination has arisen.

It is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it is not accompanied by verbal designations and lacks a deliberative mind. The object perceived belongs to the category of "real objects" (*vastu-viṣaya*).
"Real" (*vastu*) means actual. That is to say, from the real seeds produced by the mutual influence of the sense organs and their objects, there arise objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Direct perception possesses three characteristics: first, "present," which excludes the past and future; second, "manifest," which excludes seeds; and third, "actually existing," which excludes...
It has no [independent] substance. Dharmapāla says: "The five consciousnesses take only the real objects of the five sense-fields as their conditions;

they do not take the provisional *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) as their object, and are therefore called 'objective spheres' (*sva-lakṣaṇa-viṣaya*). They function spontaneously, without forming conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), and without being accompanied by names and words;

they apprehend the self-characteristic of phenomena, and are therefore called 'direct perception' (*pratyakṣa*). For example, when visual consciousness takes the four kinds of real colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—as its object..."

At that time, although the provisional forms of length, shortness, squareness, and roundness do not exist apart from the substantial form (*dravya-rūpa*), there is visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) that perceives only the substantial form of blue and so forth, and does not perceive the provisional forms of length and shortness. The provisional forms of length and shortness are perceived only by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which constructs the conceptualization of length and shortness.
As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The eye and its objects can only discern blue; they cannot discern 'this is'..."

Regarding blue: because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) cognizes blue and is also able to cognize that "this is blue," it is so designated. Furthermore, when visual consciousness takes the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the blue object as its condition, it apprehends the specific characteristic of the color blue.
However, if a subsequent moment of conceptualizing mental consciousness merely forms a cognition, it immediately carries with it names and conventions;
this is thus a common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and belongs to inference (*anumāna*). Therefore, conventional cognition and linguistic expression cannot apprehend the specific characteristic.

They function solely with respect to the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena. It is only when the five consciousnesses perceive their five respective objects that they apprehend the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a phenomenon, because they possess four attributes:
(1) spontaneity (*svarasa*), (2) direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), (3) being devoid of verbal designations (*nāma-pada*), and (4) perceiving only present objects.

Therefore, they are said to "apprehend the specific characteristic of a phenomenon. Question: By what scriptural authority and reasoning is it proven that the five sense faculties are direct perceptions?

Regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*): The answer is that the *Awakening of Great Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Mahābodhisaṃbodhi-sūtra*) states: "For example, when the light of the eyes illuminates objects before it, that light is perfectly complete and free from both aversion and attachment.
This can be used as proof that the five sense organs, in their state of direct perception, do not give rise to conceptual discrimination.

Just as the light of the eyes reaches its objects without distinction of before or after, it never abandons the hateful to take up the beloved, nor does it feel attraction toward the beautiful or aversion toward the ugly. This is analogous to the ear organ, which likewise does not discriminate.
Regarding sounds of censure and praise, the nose-faculty does not avoid fragrant or foul odors; the tongue-faculty does not discriminate between sweet and bitter tastes;
and the body-faculty does not distinguish between rough and smooth textures. This is because, at the moment of a sudden, impulsive occurrence (*sāṃvartika-citta*), there is no discrimination.

If these [sensations] flow into the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) for even a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), as soon as seeking (*paryeṣaka*) arises, they are then associated with the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
As soon as [conceptualization] arises, it falls into inference (*anumāna*), whereby defiled or pure minds arise and the emotions of grasping or rejecting emerge.

Because the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) only take the present as their object and do not take the past or future, and because they function only for a single moment, they are called "objective realms perceived by direct perception" (*svabhāva-viṣaya-pratyakṣa*).

Regarding the "three natures," these refer to the three natures of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. Question: Since the direct perception of the five consciousnesses is fundamentally devoid of good or evil, how does it relate to the eighth [consciousness]?
Since they are of the same substance and without differentiation, how can they be associated with the sixth consciousness as being of an unwholesome nature? Answer:

This refers to the drawing forth of its own seeds by the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). When arising simultaneously, all three natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral) are possible.

This speaks of the mental consciousness acting spontaneously (*anābhoga*), and does not refer exclusively to the five sensory consciousnesses. Furthermore, it is said that the fifth and sixth consciousnesses require one another.
Because it arises concomitantly with the discrimination of recollection (*anusmaranavikalpa*) and with afflictions such as anger, it is unwholesome.
Question: What is their mutual requirement? Answer: The five arise only by means of the six; the six become manifest by means of the five.
The former five serve as the gateway for the manifestation of the six, while the six serve as the basis for the discrimination of the five. This is the principle of their mutual requirement.
The three faculties of eye, ear, and body reside in two levels;
this refers to the ground where the five consciousnesses of the three realms operate and cease. The three realms are divided into nine levels.

The single level of the desire realm is called the "ground of mixed habitation of the five destinies," which possesses all eight types of consciousness. The form realm consists of four levels, namely the first... [and so forth].
The first dhyāna is the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion; the second dhyāna is the stage of joy and bliss born of concentration; the third dhyāna is the stage of sublime bliss free from joy;

and the fourth dhyāna is the stage of purity of equanimity and mindfulness. What is here called the "two stages" refers to the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion in the first dhyāna of the form realm.
This is because the five consciousnesses are fully present in the desire realm, whereas the beings of the first dhyāna heaven experience [joy] through the delight of meditative absorption.
It is for the sake of food. Because it does not consume solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), it is free from tongue-consciousness (*jihvāvijñāna*).

Since it no longer receives food, it also does not smell odors; thus, it is also free from nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*). There are only the three consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body. "Dwelling" means to abide;

this means that these three consciousnesses also abide in the first dhyāna. If one reaches the second dhyāna, which is the stage where joy and bliss arise, then the eye [consciousness] does not [function].

One sees forms, yet the ear does not hear sounds and the body does not perceive tangibles; because these three consciousnesses are also absent while one has entered meditative absorption, it is said that one "dwells" therein.

The universal, the object-specific, the eleven wholesome, the two intermediate, and the eight great [afflictions], along with greed, hatred, and delusion—this verse refers to the thirty-four mental factors that are associated with the five consciousnesses. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:

"Because they always arise based on the mind, are associated with the mind, and are bound to the mind, they are called 'mental concomitants' (*caitta*). They are established as such because they belong to the mind, just as one establishes 'mine' for things belonging to oneself."

Regarding their designations: the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) apprehends only the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of its objects, whereas the mental factors (*caitta*) also apprehend their specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).

Because they assist in accomplishing the activities of the mind, they receive the name "mental factors. Although there is no difference in the meaning of the term for all mental factors, there are distinctions among six categories:
namely, five universal (*sarvatraga*), five object-specific (*viniyata-viṣaya*), eleven wholesome (*kuśala*), and [the roots...]
There are six root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*); together these total fifty-one.

Among these, the five consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) lack only the indeterminate factors within the six categories. Regarding the "five universal factors" (*pañca sarvatraga*): "universal" (*sarva*) means all-pervasive;
"factors" (*gati*) means that which traverses or ranges over objects. Thus, the universal category possesses four kinds of "all": namely, all natures (*sarvadhātu*).
This refers to the three natures: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. "All stages" refers to the nine stages within the three realms.
"All times" refers to the past, present, future, and even a single moment. "All together" refers to the universal concomitance with the eight consciousnesses.
Question: Why do the first five [consciousnesses] possess the five universal mental factors? Answer: Because the five and the eighth [consciousness] are the same.

Substance: The fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) possesses these five factors. Furthermore, they can pervade all consciousnesses; however, since these five factors must necessarily arise whenever the mind arises, the first five [consciousnesses] also possess them.
As for the "object-specific" (*viṣayapratiniyatālambana*) factors, this is because they arise by specifically taking individual objects as their conditions.

Since the five factors beginning with desire (*chanda*) do not pervade all states of mind, they exist only within the three natures and the nine stages (*navabhūmi*), and because of the four... [text truncated].
Because their objects are distinct, they are called "distinct-object" mental factors (*viṣaya-viniyata*). As for the four objects:

they are the object desired, the object determined, the object of habitual practice, and the object of investigation. Regarding these, wisdom (*prajñā*) functions by discerning the object of investigation and severing doubt;
this is its essential nature and function. Question: Why do the first five [consciousnesses] possess all five of these distinct-object mental factors? Answer: The preceding...

Fifth, regarding the spontaneous engagement with objects: when [the sense faculties] encounter objects suddenly and simultaneously, the mental consciousness follows each perception and immediately engages in discrimination.
Each [faculty] draws forth its own corresponding seeds, and each perceives its respective object differently.

For example, the visual faculty perceiving form is different from the auditory faculty perceiving sound. Because they differ in this way for each [object], consciousness possesses these five distinct mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*).

Furthermore, those who possess the eleven wholesome mental factors do so because the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of their objective reality (*svabhāva-viṣaya*).

Question: Since the five sensory consciousnesses are direct perception of their objective reality, how can there be the root afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*), the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the two major categories, and the eighty defiled mental factors (*kliṣṭa-caitta*)?
Answer: The five sensory consciousnesses are inherently free from defiled phenomena; rather, it is by taking the five sensory consciousnesses as objects that [defilements] arise.
At that time, the sixth consciousness serves as the basis for discernment (*vikalpa*), while the seventh consciousness serves as the basis for defilement and purity (*saṃkleśa-vyavadāna*).

Therefore, it arises simultaneously with the defiled dharmas, carrying them along. As for the ten minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*), each has its own specific presiding factor; thus, they are not present here.

Furthermore, because the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) function spontaneously and lack the power of self-assertion or grasping, they do not possess the views or pride associated with the root afflictions.
Because the objects are perceived with clarity, there is no room for doubt or indeterminate cognition; thus, the five consciousnesses possess only thirty-four [mental factors].
The five consciousnesses share a common reliance upon the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*);

this verse indicates that the five consciousnesses are named according to their reliance on these faculties. The five consciousnesses receive their names based on their respective reliance on the material sense-faculties, and they fully [possess...]

There are five meanings: consciousness that relies on the faculty, consciousness produced by the faculty, consciousness belonging to the faculty, consciousness that assists the faculty, and consciousness that is like the faculty.
To say "relying on" (*āśraya*) is one of these five meanings. To say "pure matter" (*rūpa-prasāda*) is to distinguish it from the "dust-like" [sensory organs].

Furthermore, saying "relying on the faculty" is to exclude reliance on the object; the object merely serves as the objective condition (*ālambana*) and lacks the function of producing consciousness. As for...
When the sense organ (*indriya*) is impaired, even if an object is present, consciousness does not arise; it is the organ alone that can produce it. Therefore, it is said to "rely upon the organ.
It is not the "dust-organ" (*pudgala-indriya*), because the latter is a false construct subject to decay, and thus is called "floating" (*fu*).

Furthermore, it lacks the functional capacity for seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, and is therefore termed "dust" (*chen*). Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The floating-dust organ of the eye is like a reed..."
The ears are like peach blossoms; the nose is like newly curled leaves; the tongue is like two hanging melons; the body is like the crescent moon at its first appearance;
and the forehead is like a waist-drum. Because these are subject to decay and damage, they are not the bases for the five consciousnesses.

As for what is called the "pure material faculty," the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Originally based on a single brilliant clarity, it is divided into six harmonious combinations. This is because of seeing.

The essence reflects form; through the aggregation of form, it constitutes the sense faculties (*indriya*) and so forth. The source of these faculties is termed the "pure four great elements" (*mahābhūta*), and for this reason they are called "pure form" (*rūpaprasāda*).

This pure form is precisely the shell of ignorance (*avidyā*). It is also called the "ultimate faculty" (*paramārthendriya*), meaning that because these eighteen types of pure form within the eyes and other faculties are like pure *sarpis* (clarified butter), consciousnesses such as visual consciousness arise due to possessing this nature; if they were absent, [consciousness] would not arise.
It arises; it illuminates objects and gives rise to consciousness to fulfill the function of the sense organ. Therefore, it is called the ultimate (paramārtha).

Unlike the ephemeral and false [organs], which are subject to decay and destruction, this is indestructible; thus it is also called the ultimate. Unlike the ephemeral [organs], it possesses the capacity for seeing, hearing, and so forth.

Because this is capable of cognizing, it is also called "superior" (*viśiṣṭa*). It is like the eye being able to see forms, the ear being able to hear sounds, the nose being able to smell odors, the tongue being able to taste flavors, and the body being able to perceive tangibles. Question: What, ultimately, is this pure matter-faculty (*rūpa-indriya*)? Answer:
This is invisible and resistant matter (*anidarśana-sapratigha-rūpa*). Although it possesses substantial obstruction, it is not something that can be seen by the eye.
That which is known through inference is not attained through direct perception; how, then, could it be pointed out?

Nevertheless, this essence of consciousness perfectly reflects within the five gates, following the illuminating function of the floating roots. Thus, while the floating roots are five, the pure form is one.
Therefore it is said: "The root depends solely upon the one brilliant clarity.

The nine conditions and eighteen favorable signs mentioned here refer to the conditions for the arising of consciousness. All conditioned phenomena must rely on conditions to arise; thus, the eight consciousnesses now arise.
These conditions generally number nine; they differ only in that some are complete while others are deficient. Thus it is said: "Eye-consciousness arises from nine conditions;

ear-consciousness from only eight; nose, tongue, and body from seven, three, and two respectively; and the latter [mental consciousness] from five, three, four, and three. Regarding the nine conditions:
first is the condition of space (*ākāśa-pratyaya*), which refers to the absence of obstruction between the sense organ and its object, specifically the empty space within the gap.
2. The condition of illumination (*āloka-pratyaya*): This refers to the light that illuminates, such as the sun, moon, and lamps.

3. The condition of the faculty (*indriya-pratyaya*): This refers to the faculties that give rise to consciousness. 4. The condition of the object (*viṣaya-pratyaya*): This refers to the objects perceived by the various consciousnesses. 5. The condition of attention (*manasikāra-pratyaya*):

This refers to attention among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*). 6. The basis of discrimination (*vikalpa-āśraya*): This refers to the sixth consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*). 7. Defiled and pure [condition] (*saṃkliṣṭa-vyavadāna-pratyaya*).
The "support" (*āśraya*) refers to the seventh consciousness. The "fundamental support" (*mūlāśraya*) refers to the eighth consciousness.

The "condition of seeds" (*bījapratyaya*) refers to the fact that each of the various consciousnesses possesses its own specific, direct seeds. Among these nine conditions, they are subsumed within three of the four conditions:

the seeds constitute the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*); the objective condition constitutes the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*); and the remaining seven [conditions] constitute the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).

The "condition" (pratyaya) here refers specifically to the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya). Among the various consciousnesses that arise from conditions, only the visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*) is fully dependent on light;

the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) can perceive even in darkness. Excluding light, [the remaining] six consciousnesses depend on eight conditions. The three faculties of nose, tongue, and body apprehend their objects through contact; thus, they can cognize even in the dark, which is why light is excluded.
If there were a gap between the faculty and the object such that they did not meet, the body would not perceive touch, nor would the tongue [perceive taste].
The tongue does not know taste; the nose does not know fragrance. Therefore, regarding the subsequent [categories] of three, five, three, and four:

this refers to the six consciousnesses possessing five conditions, the seventh consciousness possessing three conditions, and the eighth consciousness possessing four conditions. As for the five conditions of the six consciousnesses, they are: the faculty (*indriya*), the object (*viṣaya*), attention (*manasikāra*), the fundamental [consciousness], and the seed (*bīja*).
Within the [conditions of] space and light, one further excludes discrimination (*vikalpa*), because it is the very nature [of the consciousness itself]. It does not [arise from discrimination].

It is said that "defiled and pure" refers to the faculties and objects. Regarding the seven consciousnesses having three conditions: they are the fundamental support (*mūlāśraya*), attention (*manasikāra*), and seeds (*bīja*).
The reason it does not mention the faculty and object is that they "transform in dependence upon" and "take as their object" those very things which constitute the faculty and object.

Regarding the eighth consciousness having four conditions: they are the faculty, the object, attention, and seeds. It does not mention the "fundamental," because that is its own self-substance (*svabhāva*). It does not mention "defiled and pure."

This is because they serve as the basis and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). As for "non-conceptual," it means that [the sense organs] do not take the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) as their object, because that is non-conceptual.
If one were to increase each by one equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), then the eye and the other [faculties] would constitute ten such conditions.

An equal-and-immediate condition refers to the preceding moment of each respective consciousness that has already ceased; it clears the way and induces the subsequent moment to arise, with no interval between them.

This refers to the mind in its continuous succession. The preceding thought does not depart, nor does the succeeding thought arise, because the self-substance of the preceding thought occupies its own path.
Therefore, when consciousness arises, it must rely upon these conditions.

"Combining three and separating two to observe the mundane world"—this verse describes how the five consciousnesses apprehend their objects differently. The two consciousnesses of eye and ear apprehend objects while separated from them;

the three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body apprehend objects while in contact with them. How is this known? It is said: "Knowing the location and not knowing the location" distinguishes those whose sense organs are impaired.

It is not destroyed. The sense faculties are distinct, yet consciousness follows them; the causal conditions for arising are manifested through these conditions. Consciousness is known to possess the meaning of separation and conjunction by virtue of following its conditions.
Among the nine conditions, the two conditions of space and light manifest the meaning of the sense faculty being separated [from its object].

Since the visual and auditory consciousnesses both possess the condition of space, they are cognitions of what is separate. If the condition of space were absent, the object would press against the faculty; it would not merely be...
To be ignorant and to damage the faculties is like a speck of dust entering the eye that immediately destroys it, or a loud sound reaching the ear that instantly causes deafness;
therefore, one speaks of the distinction between damaged faculties and undamaged faculties. The three faculties of nose, tongue, and body do not possess the condition of space (*ākāśa-pratyaya*);
they are cognitions through contact. If they possessed the condition of space, the faculty and its object would be separated, as in the case of the objects of odor, taste, and touch.
Because they are both unaware [of each other], the three consciousnesses do not currently possess the condition of emptiness. Thus, fragrance and stench enter the nose;
sourness and saltiness ascend to the tongue; cold and heat touch the body. These three faculties are perfectly present, clearly discerning their objects; this proves they are not destroyed.
Furthermore, the eye immediately knows in which direction the visual object lies, and the ear immediately knows from which direction a sound comes. And as for the nose...
The tongue and body do not know the location of their objects; thus, knowing the place from which [an object] comes indicates separation from cognition.

Not knowing the location of the object indicates that it is grasped through contact. The "observer" (*dṛṣṭi*) is the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*), which consists of the five consciousnesses—such as the visual consciousness—and the various mental factors (*caitta*).
The "mundane realm" (*viṣaya*) is the image-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*), namely the five sense-objects such as form and so forth.
The ignorant find it difficult to distinguish between consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the sense faculties (*indriya*).
This verse [refers to] those of the Hīnayāna who do not understand that the fundamental seeds of the eight consciousnesses serve as the conditions for the arising of consciousness;

instead, they hold that the faculties and consciousness arise from one another. Because the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the pure material faculties (*rūpaprasāda-indriya*) is subtle, they are most easily confused with consciousness.

Therefore, it is difficult to distinguish. Those who are "deluded regarding phenomena" refer to the śrāvakas; because they have only severed the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) but have not yet severed the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), they are called "deluded.
What is meant by "difficult to distinguish"? It is said: because the sense faculty (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) necessarily arise with respect to the same object (*viṣaya*).

The five consciousnesses spontaneously encounter their objects as they arise; they do not give rise to conceptual discrimination, and thus the objects are of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The five sense organs also spontaneously encounter their objects accordingly; following the force of the objects, they too are without discrimination. Therefore, it is said that they are difficult to distinguish.

Since they are indeed difficult to distinguish, what is the difference between the organs and the consciousnesses? It is said: The five organs relate to their objects like a mirror facing its reflection; although there is a thing...
Correct. Because the five consciousnesses lack the arising of attention (*manasikāra*), desire (*chanda*), and mindfulness (*smṛti*), they are non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).

Although the five consciousnesses manifest images of their objects like a mirror reflecting forms, and although they appear as such reflections, they nonetheless possess the simultaneous arising of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) along with its attention, desire, and mindfulness;

yet, because they lack the calculation of names, phrases, and categories, they are called "non-conceptual. These are the distinct meanings of the two [types of non-conceptuality]. The followers of the Hīnayāna do not understand this distinction regarding the faculties (*indriya*).

The faculties (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) each possess seeds and actual manifestations (*samudācāra*), which serve as their respective roots; thus, the faculties and consciousness arise in mutual dependence.

While it may be said that the seeds and manifestations of the faculties can only direct the seeds and manifestations of consciousness—meaning it is acceptable to call the faculties the conditions for the arising of consciousness—it is incorrect to say they actually produce consciousness.
This is because consciousness possesses its own inherent seeds capable of producing it. For consciousness is a mental phenomenon (*caitta*). That is to say:

The seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses is the faculty (*indriya*), which is a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*); this is the objective-image-division (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses.

This is the difference between matter and mind. The faculty can illuminate the object, while the consciousness can cognize the object; this is the difference in the functions of the faculty and the consciousness.
As for the statement that they are "difficult to distinguish," this refers to the Master of the Treatise’s observation that the ignorant are unable to distinguish them.

Therefore, for those whose minds are deluded regarding the mental, the World-Honored One taught the aggregates (*skandha*) to clarify it; for those deluded regarding form (*rūpa*), he taught the bases (*āyatana*) to clarify form;

and for those deluded regarding both mind and form, he taught the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) to clarify both. Is it not, then, the case that the distinction between the sense faculties (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is truly difficult to discern? As it is said:

What, then, is meant by their being difficult to distinguish? It is said: from the *Avataṃsaka* to the *Śūraṅgama*, these three categories have been expounded countless hundreds of thousands of times.
Yet even Ānanda, who possessed vast learning, still spoke of "knowing with the mind" and "seeing with the eyes.

When the Buddha questioned him as to whether the sense organ (*indriya*) itself could see, it was through this that he demonstrated how difficult it is to distinguish between the faculties (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Thus, one may observe that the faculties and consciousness are indeed difficult to differentiate.
Understood. The chapter on the tainted (*sāsrava*) is concluded.
"Transforming appearances to contemplate emptiness is solely the subsequently attained wisdom; even within the fruit, it still does not fully express the ultimate truth.

The first eight lines concern conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). These four lines of verse describe the transformation of the five consciousnesses into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

This refers to supramundane unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). First, the preceding verse [states] that the five types of transformative wisdom (*parāvṛtti-jñāna*) cannot directly take True Suchness (*tathatā*) as their object.
This is because Master Sthiramati maintains that within the first five causes, once they have become untainted (*anāsrava*), they transform their aspects to take Suchness as their object;

for he holds that the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) are of the nature of universal construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), while the self-attesting aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) is of the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Upon reaching the state of Buddhahood...
Within this [system], the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) directly perceives *tathatā* (suchness), because it lacks the characteristic of the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*).

Master Hūi (Hufa Shi) regards the seeing- and image-aspects (*darśana- and nimittabhāga*) as the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*), the sixth and seventh consciousnesses as the imagined grasping (*parikalpita-adhyavasāya*), and the self-cognizing aspect as the perfected nature (*pariniṣpannasvabhāva*);
he takes this to be the correct doctrine. Therefore, the author of the treatise refutes it with these two lines.
"Transformation" (pariṇāma) refers to the transformation-aspect (ākāra). "Aspect" (nimitta) refers to its own aspect;

that is, the aspect of the mental state which acts as the perceiver, arising as a transformation bearing the image of the objective essence (ālambana-svarūpa), and thus perceiving it—this is called the remote object-condition (parokṣa-ālambana-pratyaya). "Contemplation" (darśana) refers to the seeing-portion (darśana-bhāga) of the perceiving consciousness.
Emptiness is the suchness (*tathatā*) that serves as the object of focus. Because one apprehends suchness as bearing aspects within the first five causes, it is called "contemplating emptiness.
The term "only subsequent attainment" excludes fundamental [wisdom]. Since it is not fundamental wisdom, it cannot directly take suchness as its object.
As for the phrase "even in the fruit it does not itself designate reality," "the fruit" refers to the stage of Buddhahood.

"Quán" (詮) means "to possess. The meaning is that the five transforming consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-pariṇāma-jñāna*) do not merely fail to take *tathatā* (suchness) as their object during the causal stage;

even when in the state of Buddhahood (*buddha-phala-avasthā*), they cannot directly take *tathatā* as their object. This is because the five [consciousnesses] and the eighth [consciousness] are perfected upon the fruition.

An-hui’s calculation—that the five consciousnesses become untainted (*anāsrava*) during the causal stage—is the first error. Furthermore, he takes the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) as the basis.

Regarding "arising from others" (*paratantra*): that which arises based on the *tathatā* (suchness) of others refers to the wisdom that is accomplished through the fundamental cultivation of the dependent nature;
therefore, it is called "subsequently attained wisdom" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Consequently, it cannot directly take *tathatā* as its object.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that at the stage of Buddhahood the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) takes *tathatā* as its object—since the self-verification itself is [of the nature of] the dependent—if this were the case...
The dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) belongs to the subsequently attained cognition (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna). How could the subsequently attained cognition take suchness (tathatā) as its object?

This is another error. Therefore, these two phrases merely refute the calculations of divergent teachers. Regarding the *sākāra* (with-aspect) interpretation, the Tripiṭaka Master explains that it has two meanings:

first, "carrying along" (*kṣepa*), and second, "transformative carrying" (*pariṇāma*). Furthermore, "aspect" (*lakṣaṇa*) also has two meanings: first, the aspect of essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), and second, the aspect of phenomenal appearance (*ākāra-lakṣaṇa*). As for the term "carrying along" (*kṣepa*):...

"Directly carrying" means that fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) directly grasps the characteristics of true suchness (tathatā) as its object; thus, it takes the essence and its characteristics as its own characteristic.

"Transformative carrying" means that subsequently attained wisdom (prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna), when taking the various conditioned phenomena of the sense organs, the body, and the physical world as its objects, must necessarily carry their phenomenal marks and transform them into the essence of emptiness.
Although it contemplates all phenomena as empty, it has not yet departed from the mark of emptiness; this is merely able to [contemplate] externally.

"Taking all phenomena as objects, because they cannot directly take True Suchness (tathatā) as their object, the perfectly luminous [wisdom] first arises and becomes untainted; the three classes of transformation bodies bring rest to the wheel of suffering.

This verse describes the transformation of the five consciousnesses at the level of fruition. "Perfectly luminous" refers to the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna). Because the fruits of the fifth and eighth [consciousnesses]...
"Supreme perfection" refers to the moment when the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), the eighth [wisdom] at the stage of Buddhahood, first unfolds;
at that very instant, the fifth wisdom, the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), suddenly manifests, thereby becoming untainted (*anāsrava*). Question:

Why is it said that the first unfolding of the supreme perfection belongs to the eighth [wisdom], while the former five are called "transformed wisdoms" (*parāvṛtti-jñāna*)? Answer: Because the former five faculties are the direct [manifestations] of the eighth.

Regarding the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*): because the eighth consciousness that undergoes transformation is contaminated (*sāsrava*), and the five sense-faculties (*indriya*) that are transformed from it are likewise contaminated, the faculties give rise to consciousness.
Since the faculties are contaminated, the consciousness is also contaminated, as the fifth [consciousness] and the eighth share the same substance.
When the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) of the eighth consciousness first manifests, then the first five faculties and the five consciousnesses all become uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The outflows are immediately transformed into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). Regarding the three types of manifested bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*):
first, the great manifested body, namely the ten-thousand-fathom Vairocana, which appears in response to those on the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*). Second, the small manifested body.

This refers to the sixteen-foot golden body, which is manifested in response to those of the two vehicles and ordinary beings. Third is transformation that is indeterminate according to the species [of beings].
This means that because the Tathāgata’s vows are vast and profound and his compassion universally covers all, he responds immediately to the needs of various classes of beings as they arise.
He may manifest a large body that fills the void of space, or he may manifest small bodies of various and unequal sizes. By means of this...

Because there is external activity within the cause, the fruit brings about the fulfillment of the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (the wisdom that accomplishes what is to be done) for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.

By manifesting various supernatural transformations through miraculous powers (*ṛddhi*), it guides sentient beings out of the suffering of birth and death; therefore, it is called the "Wheel that Quells Suffering."
○ Regarding the verse on the six consciousnesses:
"The three natures, the three means of valid cognition, and the three objects are all pervasive.

This verse indicates that the six consciousnesses are all pervasive with respect to the three natures, the three means of valid cognition, and the three objects. The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes objects as its conditions and performs discrimination.
It is supreme. Therefore, all good and evil take the mind as their precursor. The mind arises with great swiftness; the mind precedes speech.
If the mind is good, then phenomena are correct; if the mind is evil, then the environment is perverse.
It is like a single breath: exhaled, it is warm; blown forth, it is cold. It is like a single body of water: chilled, it freezes; warmed, it melts. It depends entirely upon this one [mind].
The mind transforms according to conditions; therefore, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the three means of valid cognition (*tripramāṇa*), and the three objects (*triviṣaya*) are common [to all].
All fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*) are fully present. Read the word "common" (*sāmānya*) as it runs through the preceding and following sections. Regarding the "three natures":

the nature of goodness (*kuśala-svabhāva*) has the meaning of being compliant and beneficial; it accords with correct principle (*yukti*) and benefits both oneself and others. The nature of unwholesomeness (*akuśala-svabhāva*) has the meaning of being contrary and harmful; it opposes...

Regarding correct reasoning, [ignorance] harms both oneself and others. As for its indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), it is because it leaves no record within the categories of the wholesome or the unwholesome.

Regarding the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): first is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). "Direct" (*prati*) means manifesting; it refers to clearly verifying various objects without being accompanied by verbal designations (*nāman*) and without the mind engaging in conceptual estimation (*ūhana*).
Because one directly apprehends the essence of the phenomenon (*dharmatā*), it is called direct perception. Second is inference (*anumāna*). "Inference" (*anu*) means to infer...
Inference (*anumāna*) is that which is known by means of reasoning based on a preceding object. Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states that there are three types of inference:
first, inference based on the original (*pūrvavat*), such as when one has previously seen fire accompanied by smoke and subsequently sees smoke and thereby knows there is fire;

second, inference based on the remainder (*śeṣavat*), such as when one grain of cooked rice is found to be cooked and all the rest are known to be cooked as well; third, inference based on what is commonly seen (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), such as when one sees with the eyes a person going from east to west.
One knows with certainty that [the sun] has gone there; likewise, one knows that where the sun rises is the east, and where it sets is the west, because this is known through analogy.
Third is non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*): when the mind and mental factors engage an object, erroneous discrimination that does not correspond to the object is called non-valid cognition.
Regarding the "three objects," the first is the objective sphere (*vastu-viṣaya*), which is—
Real roots, objects, and the matter produced by meditative concentration arise from their own actual seeds;

these are the objects of the first five consciousnesses and the eighth [ālaya-vijñāna], as well as the objects of the sixth [mano-vijñāna] when it perceives real matter without employing names and without conceptual deliberation. These are also called "objective spheres" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*).
Furthermore, when fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) perceives *tathatā*, this is also an objective sphere, because it is directly realized. Second, those that carry [names].
The objective realm (*ālambana*) is of two kinds. First is the "true with-essence" (*tattva-sadṛśa*). This refers to the mind taking the mind as its object;

the intermediate *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) arises at both ends, appearing as it is interpenetrated by the original essence (*svabhāva*). It is thus the aspect of the essence itself. Because the subject and object are identical within a single *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part), it is called "true with-essence.
Second is the "semblance with-essence" (*pratibimba-sadṛśa*). This refers to the mind taking matter (*rūpa*) as its object; the intermediate *nimitta-bhāga*...
It arises solely from the transformation and extension of a single aspect of the perceiving *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving division);

this is the characteristic of the mental image (*nimitta*), and it is called "resembling a substantial basis" (*sadṛśa-sad-vastuka*). Third, there are two types of solitary images (*ekacchāyā-viṣaya*):

first, solitary images with a substantial basis, which refers to the sixth consciousness perceiving the shadows of past sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). Because it arises as a reflected image by relying upon those external substances, it is called "with a substantial basis. The...

Because the transformed image-part (*nimittabhāga*) also arises from the same seed as the perceiving seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*), it is called a "true solitary shadow" (*tattvika-kevala-chāyā*) and is also termed "seeming to carry a substantial basis" (*sadṛśa-sapratibimba*).

Second, there are "solitary shadows without a basis" (*asat-pratibimba-kevala-chāyā*), which are the image-parts transformed by the sixth consciousness when it takes such things as empty flowers, rabbit horns, or the past and future as its objects.
These image-parts arise solely from seeds of the same kind as the sixth consciousness itself; for originally, empty flowers and the like do not exist.

Because flowers and other such things lack substantiality [in the mind], they are called "without substance. Because they arise solely through the transformation of consciousness, they are called "solitary shadows without substance. Question:

How can the sixth consciousness be said to perceive all three types of objects? Answer: When the sixth *manovijñāna* (mentally clear consciousness) perceives the actual objects of the five sensory realms, that which occurs simultaneously with the initial encounter is termed the "objective realm" (*xingjing*). As soon as it falls into the stage of mental deliberation, one discriminates whether it is blue or otherwise.

This yellow is what is called "resembling a substantial object" (sādṛśa-sapratibhāsa). If the mental consciousness takes as its object the past, fallen-away shadows of the five sensory objects, it is called an "object consisting solely of a shadow with a basis" (sapratibhāsa-kevalavikalpa-viṣaya).
The rotation of the three realms is easy to discern because the sixth consciousness creates various kinds of karma; since its mode of revolving through the three realms is manifest and predominant,
it is said to be "easy to discern."
"Associated mental factors: fifty-one.
This verse indicates that all fifty-one mental factors are fully present in relation to the six consciousnesses. There are four meanings of "association": first, simultaneity (*kāla*).
This refers to: first, the simultaneous arising of the two; second, the same basis (*āśraya*), meaning the same sense faculty (*indriya*) upon which both rely;

third, the same object (*ālambana*), meaning the same objective sphere shared by both; and fourth, the same mode of activity (*ākāra*), meaning that the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) function identically for both.
There are three meanings of "mental factors" (caitta): first, they always arise in dependence upon the mind, for they can only arise when the mind serves as their basis;
second, they are associated with the mind, meaning that the universal factors (sarvatraga) and others are always associated with the mind-king (cittarāja), arising as a single category;
third, they are bound to the mind, because whenever the universal factors and others arise with any given mind, they belong to that specific mind.

Because it functions through attention (*manasikāra*) and so forth, it is said that there are fifty-one [mental factors]. This means that this sixth consciousness is associated with the mental factors of six stages;
therefore, it is able to grasp the cycle of birth and death within the three realms due to the preeminence of the power of karma.
Good and evil are assigned according to the occasion;

this verse describes how the sixth consciousness, along with its wholesome or unwholesome mental factors, follows objects as they arise. When encountering the wholesome, it is associated with wholesome mental factors;
when encountering the unwholesome, it is associated with defiled mental factors. Thus, the categories of the heterodox and the orthodox are clearly distinguished.
They do not become confused or intermingled; rather, when a single thought of good or evil arises, the mental factors (caitta) assemble together, following one another according to their kind.
Therefore, it is said that they are "discriminated and assigned."
"Nature, realm, and feeling—these three constantly shift and change; The faculties and the mental factors such as faith are all interconnected.
This verse describes how the sixth consciousness is constantly undergoing transformation and alteration within the three natures, the three realms, and the three types of feeling.
For example, a single evil thought may suddenly arise during a state of goodness; a single thought of sorrow may suddenly arise during a state of joy. Such is its shifting and changing nature.

[The feeling is] indeterminate. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "These six evolving consciousnesses are easily detached and unstable; therefore, they may be associated with the three types of sensation (*vedanā*).

This is because they all experience objects that are either disagreeable, agreeable, or neither. When experiencing the aspect of an agreeable object that brings gratification to body and mind, it is called pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*).
When experiencing the aspect of a disagreeable object that oppresses body and mind, it is called painful sensation (*duḥkha-vedanā*). When experiencing an object that is neither..."
That which is neither oppressive nor pleasant in body and mind is called the sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā*).

Alternatively, it is called the five sensations (*pañca vedanāḥ*), because suffering is divided into sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and pleasure is divided into joy (*saumanasya*). Thus, these three sensations associated with the five consciousnesses are termed bodily sensations (*kāyikī vedanā*).
That which is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is called mental feeling (*caitasikī vedanā*).

When unwholesome thoughts arise, the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) arise in succession; when wholesome thoughts arise, wholesome factors such as faith (*śraddhā*) likewise arise in succession.

Because these various defiled and pure mental concomitants (*caitasika-dharma*) are thus linked to the mental consciousness, they constantly [arise] in relation to the three—nature (*svabhāva*), realm (*dhātu*), and feeling (*vedanā*).
It is constantly shifting and changing;

it is alone that moves the body and initiates speech—this verse indicates that the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the sixth consciousness is most preeminent. Among the eight consciousnesses, this consciousness alone is the strongest. This is because...

Because it possesses three types of volition (*cetanā*): first, the volition of deliberation (*saṃtīraṇa-cetanā*), which is called the volition of deliberation because there is no actual performance at the time of weighing options;
second, the volition of determination (*niścaya-cetanā*), which is called the volition of determination because once the mind has reached a decision, there is something to be performed;

third, the volition of initiation (*abhisamskāra-cetanā*). "Initiation" means initiating the body, and "performance" means performing speech. The volition that initiates the body is termed bodily action (*kāyakarma*).
The volition that initiates speech is called verbal karma (*vāg-karman*). Volition itself is karma;

therefore, the volitions that set the body and speech in motion constitute bodily and verbal karma, while the preceding two types of volition constitute mental karma (*manas-karman*). Because this consciousness possesses these three kinds of volition, it is more powerful than the other consciousnesses when performing wholesome or unwholesome karma.
"Projecting and fulfilling karma draws forth [rebirth];
this verse states that the three types of karma mentioned above can project two results: projecting and fulfilling.
'Projecting' refers to how this consciousness leads the various consciousnesses to create karma; 'fulfilling' refers to how this consciousness leads..."
The first five consciousnesses fulfill the retributive fruit of the eight consciousnesses; therefore it is said: "One karma draws forth one fruit, while many karmas can fulfill it.

As for being drawn by the power of the karma that invites [rebirth]: if one is associated with the eleven [mental factors] of the wholesome state, one is drawn by wholesome karma to go to the human or celestial realms;
if one is associated with the root and derivative afflictions of the defiled state, one is [drawn by unwholesome karma].
It drags one toward the three miserable realms; it is called "dragging" because it follows like a shadow follows a form.
However, the volition that constitutes the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) is necessarily produced by the sixth consciousness.

If the volition that constitutes the completing karma (*paripūraka-karma*) arises from the five sensory consciousnesses, since the five [sensory consciousnesses] lack mental apprehension (*manasikāra*), they cannot project karma. Even if they do project completing karma, it is not [projected] by themselves.

Yes. However, it is only through the guidance of the mental consciousness (*manas*) that they can perform [karmic] actions; therefore, the five [sensory consciousnesses] also possess both wholesome and unwholesome natures.
The seventh and eighth consciousnesses are incapable of performing such actions because they are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). The section on the contaminated (*sāsrava*) is concluded.
"Initiating the first thought, the Stage of Joy; even the innate [afflictions] still manifest as latent tendencies.

This verse describes the transformation of the six consciousnesses into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*). It refers to the initial stage of transformation at the level of inferiority.

Because the sixth consciousness follows the current of birth and death, it possesses both the discriminative and innate dual attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*). If one reverses this flow and returns to the source, [it is likewise transformed].

Relying on this consciousness, one performs the contemplation of the two emptinesses of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-śūnyatā*). Now, as consciousness is transformed into wisdom, one enters the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) from the stage of preparatory practice (*prayoga-mārga*).

It is only upon reaching the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) that one destroys the conceptual grasping at a self (*vikalpa-ātmagrāha*). From the eighth stage of faith onward, one initiates the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Proceeding through the three stages of the worthy ones (*tri-kṣānti*), it is only at the initial moment of the first bhūmi that one severs the conceptual grasping at phenomena (*vikalpa-dharmagrāha*). Therefore, it is said:

The two obstacles of discrimination are absent in the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā*). The verse says "joyful," which refers to the first stage. "Initiation" refers to the wisdom of the initial transformation.
Regarding the transformation of the sixth consciousness through its three grades: the lower grade is transformed at the first stage; the middle grade is transformed at the eighth stage;

and the upper grade is transformed at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). As for those who say it is transformed at the initial [stage], it is because within a single stage there are three types of mind, namely: [Text continues...]

Entering, abiding, and emerging. When first entering the stages (*bhūmi*), it is called the "initial mind. Once the two types of conceptual grasping (*vikalpita-grāha*) have been destroyed, the two types of innate grasping (*sahaja-grāha*) then manifest;

hence it is said they are "presently active entanglements and latent tendencies" (*paryavasthāna-svapna*). "Entanglement" refers to active manifestation (*samudācāra*), while "tendency" refers to the seeds (*bīja*).

Because at the time of ascending the stages, the seeds and manifestations of the innate [grasping] have not yet been entirely suppressed or extinguished, it is said that they still "manifest as entanglements and tendencies."
"After the Stage of Far-Reaching, it is purely untainted; Observing with perfect clarity, it illuminates the great trichiliocosm.
This verse explains the meaning of the transformation of wisdom in the medium and superior grades of the sixth consciousness. "Far-Reaching" refers to the seventh stage.
The latter term refers to the stages from the eighth, ninth, and tenth bhūmis up to the position of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).

This means that although the transformation of wisdom (*jñāna-parāvṛtti*) occurs upon entering the middle grade of the eighth bhūmi, it is not yet ultimate; only at the final moment of mind prior to Equal Enlightenment does it become the highest grade.

Therefore, it is called "perfectly luminous" (*paripūrṇa-prabhāsvara*). Because all outflows (*āsrava*) are forever exhausted within this ultimate stage, the nature of the untainted (*anāsrava*) increases accordingly, and it is pure, perfectly luminous, and complete.
Upon reaching this stage, the six consciousnesses finally become purely undefiled (*anāsrava*).
They are then transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), which illuminates the great trichiliocosm with perfect clarity.

This means that the Tathāgata is skillfully able to observe the harmonious integration and sequential unfolding of all phenomena, and further knows the faculties, natures, and inclinations of sentient beings, thereby expounding various [teachings] through unimpeded eloquence.
The Wondrous Dharma causes them to attain awakening and achieve great peace and bliss; all of this is the function of the wondrous wisdom of observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).
Verse on the Seventh Consciousness:
Possessing a "substantiated" nature, it is obscured and pervades both the sentient and the fundamental. Following conditions, it clings to a self; its cognitive capacity is erroneous.

This verse concerns the nature and extent of the objects of the seven consciousnesses. Among the three types of objects, this consciousness perceives only those that are "true with a representative aspect" (zhen-daizhi).

This means that when the mind takes the mind as its object, a representative aspect (xiangfen) arises at both ends; because it arises by interposing its own aspect while simultaneously grasping the original essence (benzhi), it is called "true with a representative aspect.
The phrase "pervading both the mental and the fundamental" distinguishes this from the preceding six consciousnesses, which take the mind... [as their object].

Taking form (*rūpa*) as its object constitutes a "semblance-with-substance" (*sadr̥śa-savastu*) object. This means that this semblance-with-substance also extends to the seven consciousnesses, which are the cognizing minds;

because they constantly give rise to grasping, they are the "sentiment" (*qing*). Furthermore, it extends to the seeing-parts (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses, which are the "substance" (*ben*).
"Substance" refers to the fact that the seven consciousnesses are established based upon these seeing-parts; therefore, when these seven consciousnesses take the eighth...
The *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) of the eighth consciousness is divided into the "middle" (*madhya*) and the "aspect" (*nimitta*). This is because it is the aspect of the essence itself;
since the *darśana-bhāga* of the seventh consciousness and the essential nature of the eighth consciousness are mutually interwoven and co-arise, it is termed "true.
Furthermore, half of this *nimitta-bhāga* arises from the same seed as the perceived eighth *darśana-bhāga*, while the other half arises from the same seed as the perceiving seventh *darśana-bhāga*.

They arise from the same single type [of seed]. Of the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses, one half constitutes the first seven consciousnesses, which are of an obscured nature (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
The other half is the essence of the seeing-portion of the internal eight consciousnesses, which is of an unobscured nature (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Now, the seventh consciousness constantly gives rise to pervasive conceptualization and grasping (*parikalpita-grāha*), while the seeing-portion of the eighth consciousness serves as its own inner self (*ātman*). Therefore, it is said: "It evolves depending on that and takes that as its object."
Therefore, among the four natures, it is only the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta). If it were the unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta), it would belong to the eighth consciousness;
for being neither wholesome nor unwholesome, there is nothing to be recorded, and thus it is called unspecified.

This means that although this consciousness lacks goodness or evil, it is always associated with the four afflictions; because it obscures and covers the true nature, it is called the obscured-unspecified.

Regarding the phrase "taking what is non-measurement as measurement according to conditions," this sentence serves to distinguish it from valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If one were to say that it involves an object with substance (*saviṣaya*), it would belong to the objective domain of inference (*anumāna*).
However, because it is associated with the four afflictions (*kleśa*), it follows its conditions and grasps the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as a self.
Since it is not inherently a self but is erroneously grasped as such, it is called "non-measurement" (*apramāṇa*).
